## What is the real challenge?

**LeetCode 278 — First Bad Version.** Choose queries based on replies while respecting an interaction limit.

This LeetCode label may describe a **problem domain, engineering interface or probabilistic method** rather than a universally named algorithm. The first step is to state which contract is required.

## The tempting solution

Query all n versions one at a time. If each query talks to a remote grader, the number of calls matters more than local CPU.

## The idea worth remembering

Interactive problems separate local computation from oracle requests. A monotone yes/no response allows binary search with exponentially fewer queries.

## One mathematical expression — with every symbol explained

$$
Q(n)\leq\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil
$$

**Every symbol means:** Q(n) counts oracle comparisons for locating the first bad version in n possible positions plus a sentinel; log₂ is base-two logarithm; ceiling rounds upward. The exact bound depends on implementation and sentinel rules.

**Numerical substitution:** With 16 ordered versions and first bad at 11, ask near the midpoint: version 8 is good, so discard 1..8. Ask version 12 (bad), narrowing to 9..12. Ask 10 (good), then 11 (bad). Four queries locate the boundary instead of up to sixteen.

The substituted numbers are not decoration: if the example disagrees with the formula, the statement or its assumptions must be corrected before code is written.

## Why the method is justified

Each query splits a remaining contiguous candidate interval; a monotone predicate guarantees the discarded half cannot contain the first true position.

**Complexity or resource cost:** O(log n) oracle calls and O(1) local extra memory; n is number of candidate versions.

console.log(lowerBound([0,0,0,1,1],1));

Run this from a `.mjs` file inside this topic directory. The mathematical relation above is the key concept, while the linked helper illustrates its prerequisite.

## Which assumption makes it fail?

Do not query outside the official allowed range. A remote interaction budget may forbid linear scans even when input size is moderate.

For this topic, distinguish an **exact probability or invariant** from a single random observation or a successful local test. A test samples executions; it is not a proof that all executions behave correctly.
